The principal biomes of the world are as follows:
Terrestrial
1. Temperate deciduous forest
2. Coniferous forest
3. Woodland
4. Chaparral
5. Tundra
6. Grassland
7. Desert
8. Tropical savanna
9. Tropical forest
Marine
1. Oceanic plankton and nekton
2. Balanoid-gastropod-thallophyte
3. Pelecypod-annelid
4. Coral reef
Distribution of the terrestrial biomes of the U.S. is illustrated in Appendix D.
As a background for subsequent discussion of the more immediate environments of species that are threatened with extinction, the following is a
physical description (taken from Kendeigh, loc. cit.) of the biomes encompass-\ning North America.
Temperate Deciduous Forest Biome: In North America the deciduous forest is best developed in the eastern United States, although elements of it are mixed with conifers in the North, West, and through the mountains of Mexico into Guatemala. Mean annual precipitation for the biome in North America varies from 30 to 50 inches. In the Gulf States it is occasionally as high as 60 inches. For the most part, rain falls periodically throughout the year; in many places, precipitation also falls as snow in the wintertime. Mean monthly temperatures from North to South vary from January minimums of -10° to 60°F to July maximums of 70° to 80°F.
